 This is a draft CAREER PLAN from 2023 on the vision of how my career may unfold.
Year 1-2: Foundation Years in College

1. Year 1, Semester 1: Register for foundational courses such as Calculus, Physics, and an introductory course in Mechanical Engineering. Start attending events and meetings of professional societies and engineering clubs on campus, like the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) or the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA).
2. Year 1, Semester 2: Continue your foundational courses. This might include classes like Chemistry and Differential Equations. Start taking introductory classes in Mechanical Engineering like Statics or Thermodynamics and in Aerospace Engineering like Introduction to Aerospace Engineering or Aerodynamics.
3. Summer after Year 1: Apply for internships, research experiences for undergraduates (REUs), or summer research opportunities at MidU to gain hands-on experience. Alternatively, take summer courses to accelerate your curriculum or lighten future course loads.
4. Year 2: Register for intermediate courses in Mechanical Engineering (like Dynamics, Material Science) and Aerospace (like Space Mechanics). Start identifying professors whose research interests align with yours and approach them about potential research opportunities.
5. Summer after Year 2: Pursue an internship that provides practical engineering experience, ideally at an aerospace company.

Year 3-4: Advanced Coursework and Professional Development

1. Year 3: Take advanced coursework in your major and minor. Join a research project with a faculty member in the department. Begin looking at potential capstone project ideas.
2. Summer after Year 3: Intern at an aerospace company to gain experience in your desired field. Work on building relationships with your coworkers and supervisors as they could serve as references later on.
3. Year 4: Complete the remaining course requirements for your major and minor. Begin deciding whether you want to enter the workforce or apply for a master's degree. If you are considering grad school, start studying for the GRE and researching potential programs. Work on your senior design project.
4. Summer after Year 4: If going into the workforce, start the job application process in the spring. If continuing to a master's program, use the summer to prepare.

Year 5-6: Grad School or Entry-Level Work

1. *Grad school:* If you opt for a master's program, focus your coursework and research on areas directly applicable to the aerospace industry. Use this time to deepen your expertise.
2. *Workforce:* As an entry-level engineer, your goal should be to learn as much as possible. Understand the ins and outs of your particular job, but also seek to understand how other departments function.

Year 7-14: Work Experience and Moving Up

1. Year 7-10: Build on your work experience and start to specialize in areas you find interesting. Continue to learn new skills, both technical and managerial.
2. Year 10-14: Look for opportunities to take on more responsibility. This could involve managing a project or leading a team. Understand the business aspects of your company in addition to the technical side.

Year 15+: Founding Your Company

1. Year 15 Begin by identifying a market need that your company could meet. Develop a business plan, consider potential investors, and start building a network of advisers.
2. Year 16 and beyond As CEO, you'll need to wear many hats. You'll oversee the strategic direction of the company, but you'll also be involved in hiring, managing finances, and potentially securing further investment. Your work experience and the relationships you've built in the industry will be invaluable during this time. SPRING 2023 COVER LETTER is given below

 Below is a winter 2022 college admission essay, the beginning of this context:
 The arm is a machine that works in unison with the rest of the body to produce a force powerful
enough to completely rip a tendon or ligament off the bone. Without a basic understanding of how
the body functions and how to maximize power output, it would be nearly impossible for a pitcher
to repeat their delivery of a 90+ mile-per-hour fastball for upwards of 100 throws per game. If just
one movement is out of sync, the whole body is at an elevated risk for injury, and performance is
compromised. It is crucial for a pitcher to take the time to understand how energy transfers, not
just within the body but also onto the baseball. The delicate process between the time a ball
leaves a pitcher’s hand and the time it hits the catcher’s mitt involves many factors (spin rate,
direction, and velocity), and results can vary widely if a consistent approach is not taken. A single
finger positioned in a different location can drastically impact the intended trajectory of the ball.
For these reasons, it is imperative that pitchers are mechanically efficient and consistent.
     Similar to many sciences, pitching requires endless hours in the lab, running experiments and
refining processes until optimal results are achieved. While not a lab in the traditional sense, a
bullpen provides a controlled environment to test different variables and learn how and why
specific changes may impact pitch results. Advancements in biometric technologies within the
baseball industry have provided athletes with opportunities to learn how to achieve better results.
These advancements have yielded a plethora of new tools throughout the past decade for pitchers
and coaches to analyze how a pitcher’s mechanical delivery impacts the outcome of a pitch. As a
pitcher myself, these new technologies have allowed me to visualize specific data points and
compare them to previous results, providing feedback to me that I would not have had ten years
ago. Information provided by biomechanical technology has heightened my interest in pitching
mechanics and helped me better understand my pitching delivery. 
     Through my pitching experiences, I have learned that new data points often reveal new insights,
providing opportunities for developing into a more efficient pitcher. For example, in the summer of
2022, my coach introduced a new fastball grip to me that he claimed would increase the ball’s spin
rate and give my pitch more movement. At first, I was skeptical of the new grip because I had been
having success with the previous one, but I decided to try it anyway. The results showed an
impressive improvement, and I quickly adopted the new pitch grip. This experience taught me that
there is always an opportunity for improvement, it just depends on where you focus your efforts.
The human body is a complex machine, and biomechanical technology provides a fascinating tool
for athletes like myself to maximize movement efficiencies.
     My experience with the biomechanical analysis of pitching has sparked an interest in the
engineering field that I intend to pursue throughout my college studies and future career. I want to
use the knowledge and skills I obtain to solve critical problems that make an impact on the world.
A quote by Engineer and Professor Henry Petroski puts my aspirations into words well: “As
engineers, we [are] in a position to change the world – not just study it.” There is no use in learning
about engineering without the intention of using it to improve society. That is why I hope to work
toward solving one of the 14 Grand Challenges for Engineering. These challenges were first
introduced to me in my Engineering Design class at Oakridge High School, where I completed a
research assignment and project on the Challenges. The concepts were intriguing and inspiring to
me, and I feel this is something I can make a significant contribution to and am dedicated to
solving.
